title: TokenRepel: Generating Diverse Image SetsWithout Compromising Quality

paper.title: TokenRepel: Generating Diverse Image Sets Without Compromising Quality
paper.abstract:
Abstract We present an inference-time approach that enhances the visual diversity of image sets generated by text-to-image models,
without compromising the average image quality.
Our method leverages the intrinsic geometry of hidden representations in pretrained models
to diversify images generated from the same prompt.
First, we introduce a token repulsion mechanism that increases the angle between feature tokens across samples.
It takes a negative Riemannian gradient step on a von Mises–Fisher mixture distribution of tokens on the unit hypersphere.
Second, to preserve the quality of each output image,
we propose a token density preservation mechanism that projects the repulsion-induced prediction change onto a half-space aligned with the model’s score direction.
This encourages the updates to remain within the high-density regions learned by the generative model.
We further extend this mechanism to the output of each intermediate layer,
enabling finer-grained iterative guidance.
We evaluate our method on three types of pretrained text-to-image models.
Experiments show substantial gains in visual diversity under identical prompts,
while maintaining a comparable level of image fidelity.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in text-to-image (T2I) generation have led to unprecedented levels of visual quality [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . However, a challenge persists in the inherent trade-off between image quality and sample diversity [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Diversity, defined as a T2I model’s ability to generate varied outputs for a fixed condition, is a critical component of generative modeling. Enhancing diversity can foster creativity and provide designers with a broader range of visual choices [ 11 , 12 ] , support data augmentation [ 13 ] and test-time scaling [ 14 , 15 ] , and increase the representation of ethnicities and genders underrepresented in the data [ 16 ] . Although diffusion and flow-matching models are capable of broad mode coverage, they may suffer from “mode gravity” during inference [ 17 ] . In these scenarios, models tend to generate highly similar outputs regardless of the random initial noise, focusing on a narrow subset of the data distribution to generate only the highest confidence samples. Existing inference-time methods diversify samples by changing prompts or text conditioning [ 18 , 11 ] , optimizing initial noise [ 19 , 20 ] , or repelling image latents [ 21 , 22 ] . More recent methods intervene in intermediate features, which carry richer information about the generated content [ 23 , 24 ] . However, they treat each feature representation as a whole rather than explicitly modeling interactions between individual tokens. Token-level repulsion can act more selectively, pushing highly similar cross-image tokens apart while leaving unrelated tokens untouched. For example, a token representing a dog’s paw should be repelled from a similar paw token in another image, but not from a sky token. NegToMe [ 25 ] follows this token-level approach, but its linear extrapolation has undesirable mathematical properties, limiting its effectiveness. It also lacks an explicit fidelity-preserving mechanism, which can introduce artifacts. To address this problem, we present TokenRepel, a training-free algorithm for generating diverse image sets while preserving fidelity. To model cross-image token interactions, we represent the normalized tokens from other images as a von Mises–Fisher (vMF) mixture on the unit hypersphere. We then update each token with a negative Riemannian gradient step on this density, increasing the angular separation between similar tokens. To prevent these updates from degrading fidelity, we introduce a token density preservation mechanism. It projects the repulsion-induced prediction change onto a half-space aligned with the model’s score direction, encouraging tokens to stay in high-density regions. We further extend this mechanism to intermediate layers, allowing for more frequent and fine-grained corrections. Together, token repulsion and token density preservation increase the diversity of generated images while largely maintaining their fidelity. Our method applies to different architectures without requiring external models or additional training. We evaluate our approach on three representative T2I models: FLUX.1-dev [ 1 ] (flow-matching), SDXL [ 4 ] (diffusion), and FLUX.2-Klein [ 26 ] (few-step distilled flow-matching). We achieve a more favorable diversity–quality trade-off than existing inference-time methods. Our approach is simple and effective, with moderate computational overhead.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text:
Although diffusion and flow-matching models improve both diversity and fidelity over GANs [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] , further enhancing the sampling diversity remains a critical challenge [ 17 ] . This issue is further compounded by recent trends in model optimization, as both post-training [ 9 , 8 , 30 ] and distillation [ 31 ] have been shown to diminish diversity. To mitigate this, Datta et al. [18] use specialized LLMs to generate diverse descriptions. Harrington et al. [19] repeatedly generate image batches and update their initial noise using diversity and quality objectives. GASS decomposes image embeddings into orthogonal axes for independent prompt-dependent and prompt-independent variation [ 10 ] . Group Inference generates a large candidate pool and selects a subset by jointly considering image quality and group diversity [ 32 ] . These approaches may require external models, additional decoding, or a much larger candidate pool. Other inference-time interventions have also been proposed. Um and Ye [16] introduced guidance that moves samples beyond high-density regions. Contrastive Noise Optimization (CNO) optimizes batches of initial noise latents with a contrastive loss on their Tweedie estimates [ 33 ] . CADS perturbs text embeddings early in sampling according to a schedule [ 11 ] . SPARKE and Particle Guidance (PG) optimize batch latents with dissimilarity objectives based on inverse Rényi kernel entropy and pairwise RBF kernels, respectively [ 21 , 22 ] . Shielded Diffusion applies sparse repulsion to nearby Tweedie estimates [ 34 ] ; DSM disperses intermediate features through feature self-guidance [ 23 ] ; and Contextual Repulsion repels contextual embeddings in multimodal attention [ 24 ] . These methods generally do not model fine-grained interactions between image feature tokens or explicitly correct diversity-promoting updates to preserve fidelity. NegToMe linearly extrapolates attention tokens away from a reference image within the batch [ 25 ] , but this update can push less similar tokens farther apart. Motion Modes [ 35 ] also uses repulsion to enhance diversity in video generation. It guides each new object motion away from previously generated motion fields. TokenRepel instead repels similar hidden tokens across images using angular feature geometry, then corrects the induced predictions toward a high-density half-space to preserve fidelity. sections.heading: 3 Enhancing Image Diversity
sections.text: In this section, we present our algorithm for enhancing image diversity, as depicted in Figure 2(a) . Given a set of image token features, our goal is to have similar features repel each other. This can be visualized as an electron cloud (feature set) in which electrons (features) repel one another when too close but are otherwise unaffected. Like electrons around a nucleus, the features cannot move arbitrarily; they remain on spherical shells. This reflects the notion that the angle between two feature vectors captures their semantic similarity more faithfully than Euclidean distance [ 36 , 25 , 37 ] ; thus, repulsion should change their angle rather than their magnitudes. sections.heading: 4 Preserving Image Fidelity
sections.text: An unconstrained token repulsion can improve diversity but may move predictions away from the model’s learned distribution, reducing image quality and prompt adherence. To preserve fidelity, we introduce a token density preservation mechanism that prevents repulsion-induced updates from pointing away from high-density regions of latent space. The pretrained flow-matching model implicitly encodes a direction toward these regions [ 38 , 39 , 40 ] , which we infer from its model predictions and use to restrict the token movement. The PyTorch-style pseudocode is provided in Algorithm 2 . sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate TokenRepel on three representative T2I models: FLUX.1-dev [ 1 ] (flow matching), FLUX.2-Klein-9B [ 26 ] (few-step distilled flow matching), and SDXL [ 4 ] (diffusion). We report all results on the GenEval dataset [ 41 ] .

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: For FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2-Klein-9B, and SDXL, we use 25, 4, and 50 inference steps, and apply TokenRepel during the first 3, 1, and 5 steps, respectively; repulsion is applied in all layers, and density preservation is applied only in the early layers (first 30, 20, and downsample & middle layers). We apply TokenRepel only to the conditional branch on SDXL. We generate 4 images per prompt at a resolution of 512 and use the same initial noise across methods for each prompt. Further implementation details and parameter settings are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: For diversity evaluation, we use three metrics: (1) DreamSim [ 42 ] , trained on human-labeled data to measure visual differences, where we use the ensemble version (CLIP, DINO, and OpenCLIP; all ViT-B/16) and report the mean pairwise distance within each prompt batch; (2) Vendi Score [ 43 ] , which computes the Shannon entropy of the eigenvalues of the cosine similarity matrix of InceptionV3 features; and (3) LPIPS [ 44 ] (VGG backbone), which measures pairwise perceptual distances within each batch. For image quality, we use multiple reward models capturing different aspects: (1) HPSv3 [ 45 ] (Qwen-7B-based), which evaluates overall quality and prompt alignment; (2) ImageReward [ 46 ] (BLIP-based), which assesses overall quality and alignment; (3) CLIP [ 47 ] (ViT-H/14), which focuses on prompt adherence; (4) PickScore [ 48 ] , a CLIP-based human preference model; and (5) GenEval [ 41 ] , which measures compositionality and constraint satisfaction using a detection model.

sections.heading: 5.1 Main Evaluation
sections.text: We compare TokenRepel with training-free methods for enhancing image diversity, including CADS [ 11 ] , SPARKE [ 21 ] , Particle Guidance (PG) [ 22 ] , NegToMe [ 25 ] , Contextual Repulsion [ 24 ] , Group Inference [ 32 ] , Shielded Diffusion [ 34 ] , and Contrastive Noise Optimization (CNO) [ 33 ] . Each method has a hyperparameter that controls the diversity–quality trade-off. We sweep this parameter on GenEval for FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2-Klein-9B, and SDXL.

sections.heading: Comparison results.

sections.heading: Discussion.
sections.text: Our trade-off parameter δ \delta directly specifies the token rotation angle, making it easier to choose consistently across models, while other methods’ trade-off parameters are less interpretable, highly sensitive, and harder to select. The settings used to plot the trade-off curves for each method and model are listed in Table 6 . Contextual Repulsion and Group Inference are two strong alternatives but have their own limitations. Contextual Repulsion [ 24 ] repels text-branch representations in multimodal attention and achieves high HPSv3 scores, but shows a larger drop in text-to-image alignment, as reflected by substantial declines in CLIP and GenEval scores. Group Inference [ 32 ] is effective on SDXL, whose baseline diversity is relatively high, but yields much smaller diversity gains on models with concentrated distributions, such as FLUX.2-Klein-9B. It also requires substantially more computation. Several other methods offer weaker performance but add negligible computational overhead, making them attractive when efficiency is important. sections.heading: 5.2 Ablations and Analysis
sections.text: We conduct ablation studies and analyze the design choices of TokenRepel, including the effects of the repulsion hyperparameters, the fidelity-preserving procedure, batch size, and the number of inference steps over which TokenRepel is applied.

sections.heading: Batch size analysis.
sections.text: We evaluate TokenRepel with batch sizes from 2 to 12 using FLUX.2-Klein-9B and matched seeds. As shown in Figure 9 , the HPSv3 gap to the baseline remains relatively stable as batch size increases, DreamSim decreases slightly, and Vendi Score rises with the size of the generated set. Because DreamSim is a pairwise metric, larger batches include more image pairs, increasing the likelihood that some pairs converge to similar modes after a one-step repulsion. In contrast, the Vendi Score increases with batch size because it estimates the effective number of distinct samples in the evaluated set. This difference is therefore statistical and does not indicate that either larger or smaller batches produce a more diverse distribution.

sections.heading: Number of repulsion steps.
sections.text: We examine the effectiveness of TokenRepel across different repulsion windows, varying the window from the first 3 steps to the first 24 of the 25 inference steps of FLUX.1-dev. As shown in the left and middle panels of Figure 10 , extending this window consistently improves diversity, but the gains quickly saturate while HPSv3 steadily decreases. To explain this saturation, we measure the fraction of image tokens whose cross-image similarity exceeds the repulsion threshold at each timestep, averaged across layers and prompts. As shown in the right panel of Figure 10 , this fraction falls from around 86% at the first step and remains around 10% near the end of sampling. Early steps shape coarse global structure and contain more similar cross-image patches, so repulsion affects more tokens. Later steps refine details, leaving fewer similar tokens to repel. We therefore apply repulsion only during the first few steps, capturing most of the diversity gain while reducing the additional computation.

sections.heading: Generalization to image editing.
sections.text: We evaluate TokenRepel on KontextBench, which contains 1,026 image–instruction pairs from 108 source images. For evaluation, an LLM generates the target prompt from the source image and editing instruction. We generate four images for each image–instruction pair using FLUX Kontext. As shown in Table 2 , TokenRepel substantially improves output diversity, with only a small drop in editing quality. Its effectiveness depends on the instruction. It offers limited benefit for deterministic edits, such as object removal, but works well for open-ended edits, such as “add a cowboy hat” or generating content in the reference style. sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Although our method enhances diversity, the upper bound of achievable diversity is still fundamentally limited by the support of the training data distribution learned by the model. For example, our method is significantly more effective on the FLUX models than on SDXL. Quality preservation also varies across metrics ( Table 1 ): it is more pronounced for HPSv3 but less effective for GenEval and PickScore. In addition, the proposed quality-preserving mechanism is not directly applicable to autoregressive image generative models [ 6 ] , since their predictions correspond to probabilities rather than gradient-like score estimates.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We have presented TokenRepel, a test-time approach for enhancing the visual diversity of generated image sets under identical prompts. First, we outlined a token repulsion mechanism for encouraging patch-wise image diversity by taking a negative Riemannian gradient step on a distribution of features on the unit hypersphere. Second, we showed how to correct these perturbations so that they remain in the high-density region learned by the generative model and extend this strategy within the transformer layers. Our approach demonstrates substantial improvements in diversity of the output images across three T2I models, while largely preserving the average sample fidelity.

sections.heading: C.2 Differences from the Camera-Ready Version
sections.text: In this arXiv version, we provide more complete hyperparameter sweeps and a wider diversity–quality trade-off range for each method on GenEval. We also run all the ablations and analysis experiments on the larger GenEval benchmark (instead of DrawBench) to obtain more convincing results. Due to our limited computational resources, the setup differs from the camera-ready version as follows: • FLUX.1-dev uses 25 inference steps instead of 35. • All three models generate images at 512 × 512 512\times 512 , whereas the camera-ready version uses 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 for SDXL. • We generate 4 images per prompt instead of 6. • Token density preservation is applied to a different number of layers, which gives a better trade-off and faster inference. • We parameterize TokenRepel by the angles δ \delta and θ ¯ \bar{\theta} in degrees, instead of α = tan ⁡ ( δ ) \alpha=\tan(\delta) and β = cos ⁡ ( θ ¯ ) \beta=\cos(\bar{\theta}) , since angles directly describe the rotation and the similarity range on the unit hypersphere and are thus easier to interpret. These differences do not change the experimental conclusions.

Our method leverages the intrinsic geometry of hidden representations in pretrained models to diversify images generated from the same prompt. First, we introduce a token repulsion mechanism that increases the angle between feature tokens across samples. It takes a negative Riemannian gradient step on a von Mises–Fisher mixture distribution of tokens on the unit hypersphere. Second, to preserve the quality of each output image, we propose a token density preservation mechanism that projects the repulsion-induced prediction change onto a half-space aligned with the model’s score direction. This encourages the updates to remain within the high-density regions learned by the generative model. We further extend this mechanism to the output of each intermediate layer, enabling finer-grained iterative guidance. We evaluate our method on three types of pretrained text-to-image models. Experiments show substantial gains in visual diversity under identical prompts, while maintaining a comparable level of image fidelity. Baseline With Ours FLUX.1-dev : “A ballerina dancing in an empty train station.” FLUX.2-Klein-9B : “A girl with pink hair and a face tattoo.” SDXL : “A hot air balloon over a field of sunflowers.” Figure 1 : Qualitative results of TokenRepel on three representative text-to-image models. 1 Introduction Recent advances in text-to-image (T2I) generation have led to unprecedented levels of visual quality [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . However, a challenge persists in the inherent trade-off between image quality and sample diversity [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Diversity, defined as a T2I model’s ability to generate varied outputs for a fixed condition, is a critical component of generative modeling. Enhancing diversity can foster creativity and provide designers with a broader range of visual choices [ 11 , 12 ] , support data augmentation [ 13 ] and test-time scaling [ 14 , 15 ] , and increase the representation of ethnicities and genders underrepresented in the data [ 16 ] . Although diffusion and flow-matching models are capable of broad mode coverage, they may suffer from “mode gravity” during inference [ 17 ] . In these scenarios, models tend to generate highly similar outputs regardless of the random initial noise, focusing on a narrow subset of the data distribution to generate only the highest confidence samples. Existing inference-time methods diversify samples by changing prompts or text conditioning [ 18 , 11 ] , optimizing initial noise [ 19 , 20 ] , or repelling image latents [ 21 , 22 ] . More recent methods intervene in intermediate features, which carry richer information about the generated content [ 23 , 24 ] . However, they treat each feature representation as a whole rather than explicitly modeling interactions between individual tokens. Token-level repulsion can act more selectively, pushing highly similar cross-image tokens apart while leaving unrelated tokens untouched. For example, a token representing a dog’s paw should be repelled from a similar paw token in another image, but not from a sky token. NegToMe [ 25 ] follows this token-level approach, but its linear extrapolation has undesirable mathematical properties, limiting its effectiveness. It also lacks an explicit fidelity-preserving mechanism, which can introduce artifacts. To address this problem, we present TokenRepel, a training-free algorithm for generating diverse image sets while preserving fidelity. To model cross-image token interactions, we represent the normalized tokens from other images as a von Mises–Fisher (vMF) mixture on the unit hypersphere. We then update each token with a negative Riemannian gradient step on this density, increasing the angular separation between similar tokens. To prevent these updates from degrading fidelity, we introduce a token density preservation mechanism. It projects the repulsion-induced prediction change onto a half-space aligned with the model’s score direction, encouraging tokens to stay in high-density regions. We further extend this mechanism to intermediate layers, allowing for more frequent and fine-grained corrections. Together, token repulsion and token density preservation increase the diversity of generated images while largely maintaining their fidelity. Our method applies to different architectures without requiring external models or additional training. We evaluate our approach on three representative T2I models: FLUX.1-dev [ 1 ] (flow-matching), SDXL [ 4 ] (diffusion), and FLUX.2-Klein [ 26 ] (few-step distilled flow-matching). We achieve a more favorable diversity–quality trade-off than existing inference-time methods. Our approach is simple and effective, with moderate computational overhead. 2 Related Work Although diffusion and flow-matching models improve both diversity and fidelity over GANs [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] , further enhancing the sampling diversity remains a critical challenge [ 17 ] . This issue is further compounded by recent trends in model optimization, as both post-training [ 9 , 8 , 30 ] and distillation [ 31 ] have been shown to diminish diversity. To mitigate this, Datta et al. [18] use specialized LLMs to generate diverse descriptions. Harrington et al. [19] repeatedly generate image batches and update their initial noise using diversity and quality objectives. GASS decomposes image embeddings into orthogonal axes for independent prompt-dependent and prompt-independent variation [ 10 ] . Group Inference generates a large candidate pool and selects a subset by jointly considering image quality and group diversity [ 32 ] . These approaches may require external models, additional decoding, or a much larger candidate pool. Other inference-time interventions have also been proposed. Um and Ye [16] introduced guidance that moves samples beyond high-density regions. Contrastive Noise Optimization (CNO) optimizes batches of initial noise latents with a contrastive loss on their Tweedie estimates [ 33 ] . CADS perturbs text embeddings early in sampling according to a schedule [ 11 ] . SPARKE and Particle Guidance (PG) optimize batch latents with dissimilarity objectives based on inverse Rényi kernel entropy and pairwise RBF kernels, respectively [ 21 , 22 ] . Shielded Diffusion applies sparse repulsion to nearby Tweedie estimates [ 34 ] ; DSM disperses intermediate features through feature self-guidance [ 23 ] ; and Contextual Repulsion repels contextual embeddings in multimodal attention [ 24 ] . These methods generally do not model fine-grained interactions between image feature tokens or explicitly correct diversity-promoting updates to preserve fidelity. NegToMe linearly extrapolates attention tokens away from a reference image within the batch [ 25 ] , but this update can push less similar tokens farther apart. Motion Modes [ 35 ] also uses repulsion to enhance diversity in video generation. It guides each new object motion away from previously generated motion fields. TokenRepel instead repels similar hidden tokens across images using angular feature geometry, then corrects the induced predictions toward a high-density half-space to preserve fidelity. We report all results on the GenEval dataset [ 41 ] . Implementation details. For FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2-Klein-9B, and SDXL, we use 25, 4, and 50 inference steps, and apply TokenRepel during the first 3, 1, and 5 steps, respectively; repulsion is applied in all layers, and density preservation is applied only in the early layers (first 30, 20, and downsample & middle layers). We apply TokenRepel only to the conditional branch on SDXL. We generate 4 images per prompt at a resolution of 512 and use the same initial noise across methods for each prompt. Further implementation details and parameter settings are provided in Appendix C . Evaluation metrics. For diversity evaluation, we use three metrics: (1) DreamSim [ 42 ] , trained on human-labeled data to measure visual differences, where we use the ensemble version (CLIP, DINO, and OpenCLIP; all ViT-B/16) and report the mean pairwise distance within each prompt batch; (2) Vendi Score [ 43 ] , which computes the Shannon entropy of the eigenvalues of the cosine similarity matrix of InceptionV3 features; and (3) LPIPS [ 44 ] (VGG backbone), which measures pairwise perceptual distances within each batch. For image quality, we use multiple reward models capturing different aspects: (1) HPSv3 [ 45 ] (Qwen-7B-based), which evaluates overall quality and prompt alignment; (2) ImageReward [ 46 ] (BLIP-based), which assesses overall quality and alignment; (3) CLIP [ 47 ] (ViT-H/14), which focuses on prompt adherence; (4) PickScore [ 48 ] , a CLIP-based human preference model; and (5) GenEval [ 41 ] , which measures compositionality and constraint satisfaction using a detection model. 5.1 Main Evaluation We compare TokenRepel with training-free methods for enhancing image diversity, including CADS [ 11 ] , SPARKE [ 21 ] , Particle Guidance (PG) [ 22 ] , NegToMe [ 25 ] , Contextual Repulsion [ 24 ] , Group Inference [ 32 ] , Shielded Diffusion [ 34 ] , and Contrastive Noise Optimization (CNO) [ 33 ] . As shown in Figure 9 , the HPSv3 gap to the baseline remains relatively stable as batch size increases, DreamSim decreases slightly, and Vendi Score rises with the size of the generated set. Because DreamSim is a pairwise metric, larger batches include more image pairs, increasing the likelihood that some pairs converge to similar modes after a one-step repulsion. In contrast, the Vendi Score increases with batch size because it estimates the effective number of distinct samples in the evaluated set. This difference is therefore statistical and does not indicate that either larger or smaller batches produce a more diverse distribution. Number of repulsion steps. We examine the effectiveness of TokenRepel across different repulsion windows, varying the window from the first 3 steps to the first 24 of the 25 inference steps of FLUX.1-dev. As shown in the left and middle panels of Figure 10 , extending this window consistently improves diversity, but the gains quickly saturate while HPSv3 steadily decreases. To explain this saturation, we measure the fraction of image tokens whose cross-image similarity exceeds the repulsion threshold at each timestep, averaged across layers and prompts. As shown in the right panel of Figure 10 , this fraction falls from around 86% at the first step and remains around 10% near the end of sampling. Early steps shape coarse global structure and contain more similar cross-image patches, so repulsion affects more tokens. Later steps refine details, leaving fewer similar tokens to repel. We therefore apply repulsion only during the first few steps, capturing most of the diversity gain while reducing the additional computation. 5.3 Further Discussion Generalization to image editing. For evaluation, an LLM generates the target prompt from the source image and editing instruction. We generate four images for each image–instruction pair using FLUX Kontext. As shown in Table 2 , TokenRepel substantially improves output diversity, with only a small drop in editing quality. Its effectiveness depends on the instruction. It offers limited benefit for deterministic edits, such as object removal, but works well for open-ended edits, such as “add a cowboy hat” or generating content in the reference style.
